papers.title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions
papers.abstract: When an LLM group's discussion is compressed into a short memory for a final decision maker, what should the memory keep? Two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims relevant to the decision criteria. On hidden-profile tasks both look attractive, because how widely a fact is held is confounded with whether it helps. We introduce CrossProfile, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates with automatically verified answer keys, in which the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts is crossed while their text is held fixed (480 tasks). Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and two DeepSeek models, both heuristics fail in predictable places. Selecting by relevance readmits decoys, because decoys are on topic: even a perfect relevance filter loses 23 to 31 points to rarest-first selection in the classic hidden-profile configuration. Rarest-first selection is no better than random selection on average and wins only where the rare facts happen to be the useful ones. In both cases accuracy follows the balance of evidence the memory keeps, not the policy that kept it. The decision model adds a third failure, a form of social proof: it gives extra weight to facts attributed to many agents. Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random with line order fixed, raises accuracy in the classic configuration by 13 to 24 points. In natural discussions the evidence is lost before any memory acts: the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all.

papers.title: Where Does Rhetorical Distortion Live? A Multi-Platform, Multi-Language Measurement of Influencer Content
papers.abstract: Much of the manipulation in influencer content is not false but disproportionate, framing accurate facts as historic, urgent, or catastrophic. Existing approaches either verify factual claims or detect clickbait and propaganda in single-platform, single-language text; however, they overlook where such framing originates, because they treat a post and the replies beneath it as one unit. To address this gap, we measure rhetorical distortion with one instrument applied identically across six platforms and two languages, classifying creator posts and their replies separately. Our three-tier pipeline detects five literature-grounded dimensions (Significance Inflation, Anxiety Manufacturing, Novelty Claims, Loaded Language, and Temporal Distortion): bilingual lexical rules propose candidates, negative filters cancel known false positives, and an LLM verifies or relabels the candidates. This design keeps labels transparent and comparable across platforms, calls the LLM on only 14% of posts, and supports validation against human annotators and a second model. On 13,060 posts from 330 accounts on RSS/newsletters, YouTube, Bluesky, Reddit, Weibo, and X/Twitter, platform is far more strongly associated with account-level distortion than content category (partial $\eta^2=0.49$ vs. $0.09$), and X/Twitter scores highest (DI 7.74 vs. 0.78 for RSS). On X/Twitter, the top-5 replies under a post carry 3.5x the distortion of the tweet they answer (1.5x at equal length), while creator tweets alone are indistinguishable from YouTube and Bluesky; two human annotators and GPT-4o confirm this gap. Measured distortion on threaded platforms thus lives largely in the audience layer, which calls for measuring creator and reply text separately.

papers.title: Spectral Braids: A Topological Descriptor for Dynamic Directed Networks
papers.abstract: Eigenvalues are a workhorse of graph machine learning: spectral clustering, spectral graph neural networks, and graph kernels all summarize a network by the eigenvalues of a matrix. These eigenvalues are almost always treated as a static list of numbers. When a graph changes, however, its eigenvalues move, and when the matrix is not symmetric, they move in the complex plane, where they can wind around each other. The pattern of this winding is a braid, a classical object from topology. We propose spectral braids, a methodology for dynamic directed networks: each snapshot is aggregated into a community-level transition matrix, its complex eigenvalues are tracked over time, and the braid they trace is read off as a word. The word is then mapped to a matrix by the Burau representation, which gives a fixed-size feature vector for any classifier. The braid has a concrete meaning: each eigenvalue describes how a group of communities behaves, and each crossing records one group overtaking another. We evaluate the method on dynamic network classification, using synthetic networks of online communities whose labels describe how the network evolved between the same starting and ending states. Our experimental results show that the proposed features reach 97.1% accuracy on four classes, against 44.5% for the best feature set that does not track eigenvalues, and that the Burau features also separate networks containing the same events in a different order, which simple counts of crossings cannot do. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that defines braids and braid monodromy on graph data and uses them as features for learning on dynamic networks.

papers.title: Plan-to-Synthesis: Cross-City Human Mobility Generation via Semantic Latent Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Human mobility generation aims to synthesize realistic point-of-interest (POI) visitation trajectories and has become an important tool for travel behavior modeling, transportation management, and urban planning. Existing diffusion-based methods achieve high fidelity but require per-city generation, given the inherent heterogeneity of geospatial locations and POI categories, while large language model-based methods generalize across cities but remain too costly at scale, especially for long-horizon trajectory generation. To address this, we propose SeMoFlow, a Semantic human Mobility generation framework based on latent Flow matching. We first encode heterogeneous POIs from different cities into a shared cross-city representation space via hierarchical Semantic IDs, where shared prefixes capture transferable semantics, and successive codes progressively refine the representation toward individual POIs. Building on the semantic IDs, SeMoFlow follows a plan-to-synthesis hierarchical generation paradigm, in which an autoregressive planner generates coarse-grained semantic and recurrence patterns, and a flow matching realizer synthesizes fine-grained suffix latents. The generated latents are subsequently decoded and grounded to concrete POIs. Extensive experiments on large-scale multi-city datasets show that SeMoFlow achieves higher trajectory fidelity than existing baselines, preserves city-specific mobility motifs, and supports both joint multi-city generation and effective cross-city transfer. The code is available at \href{https://github.com/urban-mobility-generation/SeMoFlow}{https://github.com/urban-mobility-generation/SeMoFlow}.

papers.title: Decoupling Procedural and Outcome Fairness in Seed Allocation for Influence Maximization
papers.abstract: On online social platforms, equal seed access to interventions can yield unequal group outcomes through social spillovers, so an access audit alone can miss outcome disparities. We characterise this trade-off through an exact allocation-structure decomposition and a sharp first-moment floor for graph-independent seeding under additive spillovers on stochastic block networks. Decoupled Procedural Allocation (DPA) combines group quotas with selection by seeds' contributions to each group's outcome. Rankings balance total outcome against disparity, and within-quota exchanges reduce the gap. Computable bounds quantify retained total outcome. DPA achieves the smallest mean outcome gap among the compared methods at the common access tolerances on both development and prospective suites. Exposure and independent-cascade studies show how the propagation mechanism changes this trade-off. On Pokec, DPA nearly equalises modelled gender outcomes at the closest access-parity quota while preserving most of the degree-based allocation's total outcome.

papers.title: Activity-based temporal hypergraphs: from individual activity to collective social dynamics
papers.abstract: Temporal hypergraphs provide an interesting representation for many social systems, as they integrate both the temporal and group nature of social interactions. Designing models of time-varying hyper-networks yields thus a convenient way to generate surrogates of empirical social systems, to understand the mechanisms underlying their emergent properties, and to investigate the evolution of dynamical processes taking place on such structures. Here, we focus on a specific and powerful class of these models, the activity-based temporal hypergraphs. We show how activity mechanisms provide control over the time scale of the dynamics, allow high modelling flexibility, and capture heterogeneity in agents' behavior. We also highlight how the activity can straightforwardly be extracted from empirical data to create surrogate datasets. We present paradigmatic examples of such models: the higher-order activity-driven models (HADx), which show that different underlying rules for the selection of active interactions produce different higher-order dynamics; the Emerging Activity Temporal Hypergraph model (EATH), able to generate surrogates of empirical systems by using higher-order mechanisms driven by both activity and group memory. We conclude discussing future perspectives for activity-based temporal hypergraphs, highlighting the potential of this framework to bridge realistic modelling of social dynamics with the study of the complex dynamical process they can support, from social contagion to opinion dynamics.

papers.title: Moderation by Interrogation: Uncovering Concealed Intent in Agent Social Networks
papers.abstract: The emergence of multi-agent systems introduces novel moderation challenges that extend beyond content filtering. Agents with $\textit{malicious intent}$ may contribute content that appears benign to evade content-based moderation, while serving a hidden objective. To address this challenge, we introduce Bot-Mod a moderation framework that grounds detection in agent intent rather than traditional content-level signals. Bot-Mod interrogates a target agent using a fixed set of diagnostic probes and infers its intent through Bayesian posterior inference over candidate intents. It starts with a calibrated content-only prior and updates the posterior using the $\textit{likelihood}$ of each answer under every candidate intent, as assigned by the moderator, until a stopping criterion is met. To evaluate our approach, we construct Molt-Intent, a dataset derived from Moltbook, capturing diverse benign and malicious behaviors within real community structures through posts and comments. Across Molt-Intent, an external social engineering dataset, and three agent LLMs, Bot-Mod outperforms content-only moderators, a fine-tuned classifier, and judge-based interrogators both in- and out-of-distribution. On Molt-Intent, it reaches a composite F1 of 0.736 in distribution and 0.684 out of distribution, 22% and 14% above the best baseline.

papers.title: Black-Box Attack for IRS-Aided Communications with BER-Only Feedback
authors: Zhengkai Tu (The Chinese University of Hong Kong)
papers.abstract: Intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) has emerged as a promising wireless technology for enhancing legitimate communications. In this paper, we investigate an IRS-assisted multiuser MISO downlink network in which an attacker reconfigures the IRS to degrade legitimate data transmission. Specifically, we consider a black-box attack setting in which the attacker has access to neither channel information nor symbol-level observations and can observe only the BER reported by each user. The objective of the attacker is to identify an IRS configuration that maximizes the minimum BER among all users under a limited budget of non-repeated tests. To address this BER-only black-box attack problem, we propose PRIS, an online search method that learns effective phase transitions from previous trials and progressively narrows the search from large-block modifications to single-element refinement. Specifically, an annealed user-balancing reward and prioritized replay are incorporated to exploit noisy BER feedback. Numerical results demonstrate that PRIS achieves a higher minimum BER than existing benchmarks.

papers.title: What Remains Without Leaking Test Labels? Exposing Evaluation Flaws in Graph-Level Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Graph-level anomaly detection (GLAD) identifies unusual graphs in applications such as molecular screening, often using only normal graphs for training. Yet the evaluations of some detectors select models with test labels, and high benchmark scores alone do not show whether detectors recognize structural changes. We audit released code and compare the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for model states (checkpoints) chosen with and without test labels from the same training run. We separately compare test-tuned hyperparameters with repository defaults and test sensitivity to structural changes while controlling graph size. We evaluate 21 detectors on the UB-GOLD benchmark and on synthetic and molecular graphs with controlled structural changes. About half of the checkpoint-selection gain is linked to choosing a checkpoint and reporting its performance on the same labeled test set. The mean gap persists across training seeds and when normal and anomalous graphs come from different datasets. Most detectors miss many tested structural changes that simple counts detect. With tuned hyperparameters, the two leaders remain the top two by AUROC under every checkpoint rule. Across nine main datasets, test-label checkpoint selection raises the mean AUROC of UB-GOLD's 12 detectors by 5.12 points relative to the final checkpoint.

papers.title: Uncovering Non-Normality in Information Flow: Network Structure and Dynamics of Social Media Cascades
papers.abstract: Information cascades on social media are conventionally conceptualized as directed, feedforward branching processes. However, real-world diffusion pathways frequently deviate from pure hierarchical trees due to localized clustering, reciprocal commentary, and multi-wave temporal surges. In this work, we quantify the directional asymmetry and hierarchical structure of empirical information cascades on X (formerly Twitter) using spectral non-normality via Henrici's departure from normality. Analyzing approximately 58,000 cascade networks across diverse topics (including politics, entertainment, natural disasters, etc.), we investigate (1) how non-normality relates to temporal dynamics such as endogenous-like versus exogenous-like patterns and burstiness, (2) whether non-normality is correlated with the peak concentration or overall size of a cascade, (3) whether the overall non-normality of a cascade's network structure can be predicted from its early stages. We find that non-normality strongly aligns with peak concentration (peak/N) rather than overall cascade size, characterizing cascades governed by rapid, asymmetric forwarding. Furthermore, while early-stage structural forecasting (<= 30% of nodes observed) exhibits expected baseline uncertainty (51%-72% accuracy at a +/- 20% error tolerance), predictability consolidates rapidly during intermediate growth, exceeding 80% across all dynamic clusters once 50%-60% of the network is observed. By identifying the topological and dynamic correlates of cascade structures, this study advances our understanding of information flow and establishes a quantifiable benchmark for forecasting directional diffusion architectures.
